test_text.title: In search of the holy grail

article.title: In search of the holy grail
glossary: * DNA: Deoxyribonucleic acid, molecules responsible for the transference of genetic characteristics.
* eugenics: The science of improving the qualities of the human race, especially the careful selection of parents.

items.sentence_raw: It has been called the Holy Grail of modern biology.
Costing more than £2 billion, it is the most ambitious scientific project since the Apollo programme that landed a man on the moon.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says the project is *'the most ambitious scientific project since the Apollo programme'* — **'since'** here means it is the biggest project after that one. So the passage compares the Project in scale to the **Apollo programme**.

items.sentence_raw: And it will take longer to accomplish than the lunar missions, for it will not be complete until early next century.
items.explain: Q28: The passage states it *'will not be complete until early next century'* — **'complete'** means finished, which matches the question's **'completion date'**. So the possible completion date is **early next century**.

items.sentence_raw: Even before it is finished, according to those involved, this project should open up new understanding of, and new treatments for, many of the ailments that afflict humanity.
items.explain: Q33: The passage reports that *'according to those involved, this project should open up new understanding of... many ailments'* — this is a hope for the future, not a fact or fear. So the statement represents the writer's reporting of **long-term hopes**.

items.sentence_raw: As a result of the Human Genome Project, there will be new hope of liberation from the shadows of cancer, heart disease, autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, and some psychiatric illnesses.
The objective of the Human Genome Project is simple to state, but audacious in scope: to map and analyse every single gene within the double helix of humanity's DNA*.
items.explain: Q34: The passage states the objective is *'to map and analyse every single gene within the double helix'* — this is a plain description of the project's goal. So it is the writer's reporting of **facts**.

items.sentence_raw: The project will reveal a new human anatomy - not the bones, muscles and sinews, but the complete genetic blueprint for a human being.
Those working on the Human Genome Project claim that the new genetical anatomy will transform medicine and reduce human suffering in the twenty-first century.
But others see the future through a darker glass, and fear that the project may open the door to a world peopled by Frankenstein's monsters and disfigured by a new eugenics*.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says *'others see the future through a darker glass, and fear that the project may open the door to... Frankenstein's monsters'* — **'others'** means not the writer, but other people. So this represents **other people's fears**.

items.sentence_raw: The genetic inheritance a baby receives from its parents at the moment of conception fixes much of its later development, determining characteristics as varied as whether it will have blue eyes or suffer from a life-threatening illness such as cystic fibrosis.
The human genome is the compendium of all these inherited genetic instructions.
Written out along the double helix of DNA are the chemical letters of the genetic text, it is an extremely long text, for the human genome contains more than 3 billion letters.
On the printed page it would fill about 7,000 volumes.
items.explain: Q29: The passage directly says *'On the printed page it would fill about 7,000 volumes'* — **'volumes'** means books. So to write it out would require **7,000** books.

items.sentence_raw: Yet, within little more than a decade, the position of every letter and its relation to its neighbours will have been tracked down, analysed and recorded.
items.explain: Q36: The passage explains that *'the position of every letter and its relation to its neighbours will have been tracked down, analysed and recorded'* — this is a factual description of the mapping work. So it is the writer's reporting of **facts**.

items.sentence_raw: Considering how many letters there are in the human genome, nature is an excellent proof-reader.
But sometimes there are mistakes.
An error in a single 'word' - a gene - can give rise to the crippling condition of cystic fibrosis, the commonest genetic disorder among Caucasians.

Errors in the genetic recipe for haemoglobin, the protein that gives blood its characteristic red colour and which carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body, give rise to the most common single gene disorder in the world: thalassaemia.
More than 4,000 such single-gene defects are known to afflict humanity.
The majority of them are fatal; the majority of the victims are children.

None of the single-gene disorders is a disease in the conventional sense, for which it would be possible to administer a curative drug: the defect is pre-programmed into every cell of the sufferer's body.
items.explain: Q30: The passage explains that single-gene disorders are not *'a disease in the conventional sense'* for which you can give a drug — **'conventional sense'** means the usual meaning. So strictly speaking, it is not a **disease**.

items.sentence_raw: But there is hope of progress.
In 1986, American researchers identified the genetic defect underlying one type of muscular dystrophy.
items.explain: Q31: The passage says the first success was in 1986 when researchers *'identified the genetic defect underlying one type of muscular dystrophy'* — **'identified'** means discovered the cause. So the first success was finding the cause of one form of **muscular dystrophy**.

items.sentence_raw: In 1989, a team of American and Canadian biologists announced that they had found the site of the gene which, when defective, gives rise to cystic fibrosis.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says the second success was in 1989 when biologists *'found the site of the gene which... gives rise to cystic fibrosis'* — **'gives rise to'** means causes. So the second success was to find the cause of **cystic fibrosis**.

items.sentence_raw: Indeed, not only had they located the gene, they had analysed the sequence of letters within it and had identified the mistake responsible for the condition.
At the least, these scientific advances may offer a way of screening parents who might be at risk of transmitting a single-gene defect to any children that they conceive.

Foetuses can be tested while in the womb, and if found free of the genetic defect, the parents will be relieved of worry and stress, knowing that they will be delivered of a baby free from the disorder.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says that if a foetus is tested and found free of the defect, *'the parents will be relieved of worry and stress'* — this is a future hope for the project's benefit. So it represents the writer's reporting of **long-term hopes**.

items.sentence_raw: In the mid-1980s, the idea gained currency within the scientific world that the techniques which were successfully deciphering disorder-related genes could be applied to a larger project: if science can learn the genetic spelling of cystic fibrosis, why not attempt to find out how to spell 'human'?
Momentum quickly built up behind the Human Genome Project and its objective of 'sequencing' the entire genome - writing out all the letters in their correct order.
But the consequences of the Human Genome Project go far beyond a narrow focus on disease.
Some of its supporters have made claims of great extravagance - that the Project will bring us to understand, at the most fundamental level, what it is to be human.

Yet many people are concerned that such an emphasis on humanity's genetic constitution may distort our sense of values, and lead us to forget that human life is more than just the expression of a genetic program written in the chemistry of DNA.
items.explain: Q38: The passage says *'many people are concerned that such an emphasis... may distort our sense of values'* — **'many people'** means others, not the writer. So this is **other people's fears** about defining 'human' only by physical data.

items.sentence_raw: If properly applied, the new knowledge generated by the Human Genome Project may free humanity from the terrible scourge of diverse diseases.
But if the new knowledge is not used wisely, it also holds the threat of creating new forms of discrimination and new methods of oppression.
items.explain: Q39: The passage warns that if knowledge is not used wisely, it holds *'the threat of creating new forms of discrimination'* — the writer uses **'threat'**, showing this is the writer's own worry. So this represents the **writer's fears**.

items.sentence_raw: Many characteristics, such as height and intelligence, result not from the action of genes alone, but from subtle interactions between genes and the environment.

What would be the implications if humanity were to understand, with precision, the genetic constitution which, given the same environment, will predispose one person towards a higher intelligence than another individual whose genes were differently shuffled?

Once before in this century, the relentless curiosity of scientific researchers brought to light forces of nature in the power of the atom, the mastery of which has shaped the destiny of nations and overshadowed all our lives.
The Human Genome Project holds the promise that, ultimately, we may be able to alter our genetic inheritance if we so choose.
But there is the central moral problem: how can we ensure that when we choose, we choose correctly?
That such a potential is a promise and not a threat?
We need only look at the past to understand the danger.
items.explain: Q40: The passage ends by saying *'We need only look at the past to understand the danger'* — the writer uses **'we'** and **'danger'**, showing this is a personal warning. So this represents the **writer's fears**.
